steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using deep learning to model the collective behaviour of pairs of fish. It should motivate machine learning as an alternative to analytical models, point out that models are rarely tested over long timescales, and summarise what we contribute.

- Better tracking data and data-driven models; the cost of analytical modelling
- Machine learning as an alternative: pros and cons
- Evaluation of models: short vs long timescales
- Our contribution: deep network model of fish pairs, benchmark, methodology

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Collective behaviour in animal groups is a very active research field. It studies the basic mechanisms by which individuals coordinate their actions and self-organise. A very common form of collective behaviour is seen in fish schools and bird flocks, which are able to coordinate their movements together to escape predator attacks or to improve their foraging efficiency. This coordination at the level of the group mainly comes from the social interactions between the individuals. So important steps for understanding these collective phenomena are to characterise these interactions and to understand how individuals integrate the interactions with the other members of the group.

New tracking techniques and new tools for behavioural analysis have been developed, and they have greatly improved the quality of the collective motion data. Also, advances in computing have made it possible to develop data-oriented model generation techniques that are computationally demanding, and then to simulate biological models. The result is more realistic models that try to recover the social interactions that govern collective behaviours. But the bottleneck with most of these approaches is that they need demanding and laborious mathematical work to get the interactions out of the experimental data.

An alternative to these analytical models is to use machine learning (ML) techniques and let an algorithm learn the interactions directly from the data. The know-how needed for these techniques is different from the know-how needed to design analytical models. Still, the structure of the ML algorithm, here a neural network, has an impact on how well it models, and it requires specific expertise. Once the architecture is set, ML can often process data for different species without any structural adaptation and can generate new models quickly. This is very different from analytical models, where for each new species the model has to be redefined nearly from scratch. The downside of this flexibility is that ML models are usually less explainable (a "black box"). However recent ML algorithms give higher-level information that can be mapped to more tangible formats, such as force maps, which show the strength and direction of the behavioural changes an individual experiences when it interacts with other individuals in a moving group. Even with their limited explainability, ML algorithms need only a few biological assumptions. They give an almost hypothesis-free procedure that can even do better than human experts at detecting subtle patterns, and this makes ML a very appealing approach that is complementary to analytical models.

For both analytical and ML models, several studies evaluate the models over short timescales and with instantaneous quantities like speed, acceleration, distance and angle to objects, or by measuring the error between the predictions and the ground truth. Long timescales have only been considered more recently. But a model that does well at short timescales compared to experiment does not necessarily do well at long timescales. This is especially true for models that try to reproduce complex collective phenomena in living systems. As far as we know, the predictive capacity of ML models in this context has not been evaluated over both short and long timescales, meaning their ability to generate synthetic data that replicate the outcomes of social interactions over both timescales.

In this paper we show that ML models can generate realistic synthetic data with minimal biological assumptions, and that they make it possible to accelerate and generalise the process of modelling collective behaviour. More specifically, we present a social interaction model based on a deep neural network that captures both the short-term and the long-term dynamics seen in schooling fish. We apply it to pairs of rummy-nose tetra (Hemigrammus rhodostomus) swimming in a circular tank, and we show that it can also be applied to fish species with similar burst-and-coast swimming (zebrafish; Danio rerio). We benchmark our ML model against the state-of-the-art analytical model for this species, and it performs as well as that model, even for very subtle quantities measured in the experiments. We also introduce a systematic methodology to stringently test the results of an analytical or ML model against experiment, at different timescales, in the context of animal collective motion.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Collective behaviour in animal groups is a very active field of research, which studies the fundamental mechanisms by which individuals coordinate their actions [1,2,3] and self-organise [4,5]. One of the most common forms of collective behaviour can be seen in schools of fish and flocks of birds, which are able to coordinate their movements to collectively escape predator attacks or improve their foraging efficiency [6,7]. This group-level coordination mainly results from the social interactions between individuals. Important steps to understand these collective phenomena are therefore to characterise these interactions and to understand how individuals integrate interactions with other group members [8,9,10,11,12].

New tracking techniques and tools for behavioural analysis have been developed that greatly improved the quality of collective motion data [13,14,15,16,17,18,19]. In particular, advances in computing have allowed the development of computationally demanding data-oriented model generation techniques [12,20,21,22,23,24] and the subsequent simulation of biological models [25]. This has led to more realistic models that attempt to recover the social interactions governing collective behaviours. Yet the bottleneck of most of these approaches is that they rely on demanding and laborious mathematical work to obtain the interactions from experimental data.

An alternative to such analytical models is to exploit machine learning (ML) techniques and let an algorithm learn the interactions directly from data. The know-how required for these techniques differs from the one needed to design analytical models. Nevertheless, the structure of ML algorithms, here a neural network, has an impact on modelling performance and requires specific expertise [26]. Once the architecture of an ML algorithm is set, ML can often process data for different species without structural adaptation and generate new models quickly, which is very different from analytical models, where each new species requires redefining the model nearly from scratch. The downside of this flexibility is that ML models are usually less explainable ("black box"). Yet recent ML algorithms provide higher-level information that can be mapped to more tangible formats, such as force maps, which show the strength and direction of the behavioural changes experienced by an individual when interacting with other individuals in a moving group [23,24]. Despite their limited explainability, ML algorithms require only a few biological assumptions. They offer an almost hypothesis-free procedure [27] that can even outperform human experts in detecting subtle patterns [28], making ML a very appealing complementary approach to analytical models.

For both analytical and ML models, several studies evaluate models over short timescales and through instantaneous quantities such as speed, acceleration, distance and angle to objects [29,22], or by measuring the error between predictions and ground truth [23,30,31]. Only recently have long timescales also been considered [21]. However, a model that performs well at short timescales compared to experiment does not necessarily perform well at long timescales, especially when it tries to reproduce complex collective phenomena in living systems. To our knowledge, the predictive capacity of ML models in this context, that is, their ability to generate synthetic data replicating the outcomes of social interactions, has not been evaluated over both short and long timescales.

Here, we demonstrate that ML models can generate realistic synthetic data with minimal biological assumptions, and that they allow us to accelerate and generalise the process of collective behaviour modelling. More specifically, we present a social interaction model using a deep neural network that captures both the short- and long-term dynamics observed in schooling fish. We apply our approach to pairs of rummy-nose tetra (Hemigrammus rhodostomus) swimming in a circular tank, and show that it can also be applied to fish species with similar burst-and-coast swimming (zebrafish; Danio rerio). Our ML model is benchmarked against the state-of-the-art analytical model for this species [32] and performs as well as the latter, even for very subtle quantities measured in the experiments. Moreover, we introduce a systematic methodology to stringently test the results of an analytical or ML model against experiment, at different timescales, in the context of animal collective motion.
